page.eyebrow: Epic #734 · Wave 2 · first of the three appendices
page.title: The Balaji Reddie appendix against Neave's PDF
page.standfirst_html:
Every text flag the comparator raised for Contributions from Balaji Reddie, adjudicated against Q.Contributions.from.Balaji.Reddie.11Sep21.pdf — the extracted text for wording, eleven page images, and the PDF's own font data for every italic run. On its flag counts this looked like the lightest record left: 141 flagged sentences, 34 near-certain, 2 reference mismatches, and a 72% clean rate, the highest of the eighteen.

The counts were misleading, and the reason is worth more than any single fix below. This record carries a different kind of defect from the twelve days. Not drifted punctuation and stale page pointers, but whole paragraphs absent and single words swapped for plausible-looking ones that invert the sentence. The site tells the reader the commute's process limits are “0 and 40 minutes” — a pair of numbers that appear nowhere in the source, and that contradict the next paragraph, where 40 minutes is “way above the upper process limit”. It says “You may have to do it on Day 3” where Neave wrote “You saw how to do it on Day 3”. “faintly possible” reads “fairly possible”, which reverses it; “mere information” reads “more information”, which destroys the information-versus-knowledge distinction the next line then states.

Four runs of source paragraphs are simply absent, about 450 words in all. Two of them close printed page 2 and open page 3 — the passage that takes Reddie's argument out to industry, the market, the world, and then the family. The site later says “We have seen that, since a family is a system…”, referring back to a passage the reader was never shown. A third loses the definition of “intrinsic motivator”, a term Prelude D then leans on repeatedly.

The validator reported one missing paragraph, and it was a table row. None of the four dropped runs reached its missing detector: each found a loose match elsewhere in its own chapter and so cleared the floor, surfacing as ordinary low-similarity noise. They were found by reading the source through against the site. See S-05 — it bears on how the remaining two appendices should be worked.

sections.title: Fix proposed
sections.note_html: Ordered by source page. Q-01 and Q-02 are one continuous run of four dropped paragraphs split across two source pages — accept or decline them together. Findings sharing a line number sit in the same sentence and would be applied in one edit.

items.flag: Altered flag — see the report's Altered section
items.source_html:
Two full paragraphs close printed p2, after “We mean ‘help the system as best it can to try to achieve its aim’.”:

So, thinking in terms of optimising the system, i.e. positively, no one component in any gadget is more important than any other: they are interconnected. In industry, again thinking positively, no one function is more important than any other: they are interconnected. In the market, thinking positively, no one organisation is more important than any other: they are interconnected. In the world, thinking positively, no one country is more important than any other: they are interconnected.

Further, thinking positively, is this not also the truth with individuals? A family is a system. Could you point a finger at one of them and say that he or she is the “most important” member of the family? Could you? At first, the answer to that question may seem paradoxical—but give it time! If you realise that you cannot choose the “most important” member then you’re thinking positively, i.e. in terms of optimising the system.
items.site_html: <mark class='gone'>Neither paragraph appears anywhere in the chapter.</mark> The site runs straight from “… try to achieve its aim” (line 41) to “Let’s consider a further example of interconnectedness” (line 43), which is printed p3 material.
items.evidence_html: Verified on the page image for PDF p6, whose footer reads “Contributions from Balaji Reddie : page 2”. This is the ladder that carries Reddie's argument out from the body to industry, the market and the world, and then to the family. The site later refers back to it. Line 67 reads “We have seen that, since a family is a system, it is silly to talk of the ‘most important’ member of the family” — a back-reference to a passage the reader was never shown. That is what makes this an accidental omission rather than an editorial cut.

items.flag: Altered flag — see the report's Altered section
items.source_html:
Two further paragraphs open printed p3, immediately after the two above:

But if you believe that you can do so (i.e. one person is most important, all the others are less so), you’re thinking negatively. Which way do you prefer to think? From his answer to that question about the “most important” part of a system, Dr Deming’s preference is clear.

We can take our reasoning yet a further step forward. Not only do different parts of a system exist for each other—they also exist because of each other. Every part of a system has an identity both for and because of the other parts of the system—it’s a two-way interconnectedness. So, thinking positively yet again, isn’t it wrong, illogical and foolish to try to choose the “most important” part of any system?
items.site_html: <mark class='gone'>Neither paragraph appears anywhere in the chapter.</mark> Same gap as the finding above — the four run consecutively in the source.
items.evidence_html: Verified on the page image for PDF p7. Listed separately from the previous finding because they sit on a different source page, but they are one continuous run of dropped text and should be restored together. The second paragraph states the two-way interconnectedness idea that line 45 then calls back to: “This example also provides another illustration of different parts of a system each having an identity both for and because of each other” — ‘another’ pointing at an illustration the site never gave.

items.proposal: We have already argued that (thinking positively about optimisation) it does not make sense to choose a "most important" part of a system

items.flag: Altered flag — see the report's Altered section
items.source_html: I’ve found that, on average, it takes me 20 minutes to drive to work, and that the lower and upper process limits, <mark class='src'>i.e. the anticipated minimum and maximum times,</mark> are 15 and 25 minutes respectively.

The very next paragraph reads “it took me 40 minutes to get there… Since 40 minutes is way above the upper process limit”. With the site's text, 40 minutes is the upper process limit, so the worked example that follows makes no sense. The source's own parenthetical does something quite different: it glosses what a process limit is.
items.proposal: I've found that, on average, it takes me 20 minutes to drive to work, and that the lower and upper process limits, i.e. the anticipated minimum and maximum times, are 15 and 25 minutes respectively.

items.flag: Altered flag — see the report's Altered section
items.source_html: <mark class='src'>There is</mark> a collection of common causes, <mark class='src'>often very many of them,</mark> for the behaviour of any process…

items.evidence_html: Two substitutions in one sentence. ‘These are a collection’ has no antecedent and disagrees in number; ‘often varying by many of them’ is not a meaningful phrase. The source's point is simply that a process has many common causes.
items.proposal: There is a collection of common causes, often very many of them, for the behaviour of any process, and no value within its process limits can be regarded as unusual.

items.flag: Altered flag — see the report's Altered section

items.flag: Altered flag — see the report's Altered section
items.source_html: … when those numbers are in effect simply being produced by the process or the system within which they are working.
items.site_html: … when those numbers are being produced by the process or the system within which they are working.
items.evidence_html: The dropped qualifier is the claim. Without ‘in effect simply’ the sentence asserts that the process literally produces the numbers; with it, Reddie is saying the numbers are attributable to the process rather than the person, which is the section's entire argument.
items.proposal: But it just isn't logical to make comparisons between two numbers and judge people accordingly when those numbers are in effect simply being produced by the *process* or the *system* within which they are working.

items.flag: Altered flag — see the report's Altered section

items.site_html: … and processes keep on fluctuating. The system’s output, i.e. its “performance”, is also never constant but keeps changing.
items.evidence_html: A whole sentence dropped, plus the inference marker that followed it. The dropped sentence is the link in the argument — it is why the system's output must vary — and ‘So it must follow that’ is what marks the next sentence as a conclusion rather than a restatement.
items.proposal: and processes keep on fluctuating. The system's overall output depends in some way on all of these very numerous fluctuations. So it must follow that the system's output, i.e. its "performance", is also never constant but keeps changing.

items.flag: Altered flag — see the report's Altered section
items.source_html: Children ask questions simply because they want to know, they are curious, <mark class='src'>they want to learn, they enjoy learning. These are “intrinsic motivators”. Unlike extrinsic motivators, intrinsic motivators are intimately</mark> connected with the questions and the learning.
items.site_html: Children ask questions simply because they want to know, they are curious, <mark class='gone'>they are intrinsically</mark> connected with the questions and the learning.
items.evidence_html: Verified on the page image for PDF p23. Two whole sentences are gone and the surviving halves have been spliced into one. What is lost is the definition of ‘intrinsic motivator’ itself — the term is introduced nowhere else in the Preludes, yet Prelude D goes on to use it repeatedly (“fostering and building upon people's intrinsic motivation”) and to contrast it with the extrinsic motivators defined two sentences earlier. The spliced result is also simply false about children: they are not ‘intrinsically connected with the questions’; the motivators are.
items.proposal: Children ask questions simply because they want to know, they are curious, they want to learn, they enjoy learning. These are "intrinsic motivators". Unlike extrinsic motivators, intrinsic motivators are intimately connected with the questions and the learning.

items.evidence_html: The most useful thing this pass learned, and it is about the tool rather than the text. None of the four dropped-paragraph findings above (Q-01, Q-02, Q-21, Q-29) reached the missing detector. Each dropped paragraph found some loose match elsewhere in its chapter — “A family is a system” scored against “Sugar is a hydrocarbon” — and so cleared the 0.40 missing floor and was reported as a low-similarity altered flag instead, indistinguishable from the ordinary noise at that end of the distribution. They were found by reading the source top to bottom against the site, not by working the flag list. The same should be assumed necessary for appendix-main and appendix-optional-extras, and it is worth asking whether the twelve day passes, which did work from the flag list, have the same blind spot. No change proposed here — it wants its own issue.
